summary: SRv6 steers packets using a list of 128-bit segment identifiers in the IPv6 header. This RFC defines new flavors of the SRv6 endpoint behaviors from RFC 8986 that compress the segment list, greatly reducing the encapsulation size needed to express a path.

plainLanguage.summary: A long list of directions takes lots of space on a packet. This writes the directions in a shorthand to make the packet lighter.

questions: what is the difference between next-csid and replace-csid
how does srv6 segment list compression work
subtitle: A way to squeeze a long SRv6 path into far fewer bytes by packing many short SIDs into each 128-bit slot.

tldr.problem: SRv6 steers a packet along a path using a list of 128-bit segment identifiers. Long paths mean long lists, and every entry repeats the same leading bits and wastes trailing padding bits.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9800 defines two new flavors of the RFC 8986 endpoint behaviors, NEXT-CSID and REPLACE-CSID. Both pack several short compressed SIDs (CSIDs) behind one shared Locator-Block, and the endpoint node swaps in the next CSID as the packet moves along.
tldr.outcome: The packet header shrinks significantly for long segment lists while the Destination Address always stays a valid SRv6 SID. The RFC also updates RFC 8754 so an SRH Segment List entry may be a packed REPLACE-CSID container.

today: RFC 9800 is a Proposed Standard from June 2025. It is not obsoleted by any later RFC in the unit metadata, and it updates RFC 8754 by allowing REPLACE-CSID containers in the SRH Segment List.

sections.title: Why Compress the Segment List
sections.content:
Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) lets a source node program a path by listing segments. RFC 8986 builds on the IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH) from RFC 8754 to define topological and service segments. Some applications, such as strict path traffic engineering, may need long segment lists.

Compressing the encoding of those lists can significantly reduce the header size. This RFC does that with new flavors of the existing endpoint behaviors, plus two new behaviors that keep compression efficient across several routing domains. It is compatible with the SRv6 control plane extensions for IS-IS, OSPF and BGP.

The compression works because all SIDs from the same Locator-Block share their most significant bits, and SIDs shorter than 128 bits are padded with zeros. Compression avoids repeating the Locator-Block and reduces the padding.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet carries a list of places to visit, and every place is written in a very long address. This RFC finds a shorter way to write the list so the packet is lighter.

sections.title: New Terms and SID Parts
sections.content:
A SID is split into a Locator-Block (the most significant bits, shared by the whole SID block), a Locator-Node (identifies the endpoint node), a Function and an Argument. Their lengths are written LBL, LNL, FL and AL. The Locator-Node and Function together are the CSID (Compressed-SID), and their combined length is LNFL, also called the CSID length.

A CSID container is a 128-bit IPv6 address holding one or more CSIDs and the Argument of the last one. A CSID sequence is a group of consecutive list entries that share one Locator-Block. A compressed SID list mixes CSID sequences with zero or more uncompressed SIDs.

For handing out CSID values, a deployment may split the number space into a Global Identifiers Block (GIB) and a Local Identifiers Block (LIB).
sections.plainLanguage: An address has a city part, a street part and some spare room. The city part is the same for everyone nearby, so you can write it once and keep only the short street part for each stop.

sections.title: The NEXT-CSID Flavor
sections.content:
With NEXT-CSID, each CSID container is a fully formed 128-bit SID. It holds the common Locator-Block, then the first CSID as its Locator-Node and Function, and then the following CSIDs packed one after another into its Argument. With equal-length CSIDs a container carries up to K CSIDs, where K is floor((128-LBL)/LNFL). Each NEXT-CSID container is independent of the others.

At an endpoint SID, if the Argument is non-zero, the node checks the Hop Limit, copies the whole Argument into the bits right after the Locator-Block, zero-fills the rest, decrements the Hop Limit and forwards. The Segments Left field is not changed. If the Argument is 0, the node falls back to the usual behavior and copies the next Segment List entry from the SRH.

An implementation MUST support a 32-bit LBL and a 16-bit CSID length for NEXT-CSID, and MAY support others. It MUST accept any Argument value for such a SID. The RFC's example packs eight CSIDs (48-bit block, 16-bit CSIDs) into two containers of five and three.

The flavor is defined for End, End.X, End.T, End.B6.Encaps, End.B6.Encaps.Red and End.BM. The PSP, USP and USD flavors are unchanged when combined with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The first stop's address carries a little train of short house numbers behind it. At each stop, the next number slides to the front and the rest of the train shuffles up.

sections.title: The REPLACE-CSID Flavor
sections.content:
With REPLACE-CSID, only the first element of a CSID sequence is a fully formed SID. Its Argument holds an index that starts at 0. The following entries are CSID containers in packed format: 128-bit SRH Segment List entries cut into K positions of LNFL bits, with K = floor(128/LNFL), carrying only CSIDs and no Locator-Block. The second CSID sits in the least significant position (K-1), the third in K-2, and so on.

At each hop the endpoint node decrements the index. When the index reaches 0 it decrements Segments Left and resets the index to K-1. It then copies the next CSID from the packed container into the bits after the Locator-Block of the Destination Address. The Destination Address therefore always remains a valid SRv6 SID, and a packed entry is never copied to it as is.

The flavor is defined for 16-bit and 32-bit CSID lengths, and an implementation MUST support a 32-bit one. It covers End, End.X, End.T, End.B6.Encaps, End.B6.Encaps.Red and End.BM, and also the End.DX and End.DT family. For those last ones the Argument is ignored, except that End.DT2M reads a 16-bit Arg.FE2 from a defined place.

This is the change that updates RFC 8754: a Segment List entry may now be either an IPv6 address or a REPLACE-CSID container in packed format. The special CSID value 0 ends a sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the first stop has an address, and the next stops are written in a compact notebook page with several short numbers per line. A little counter says which number to use next.

sections.title: CSID Allocation and FIB Entries
sections.content:
The CSID value 0 is reserved and marks the end of a CSID container. A global CSID comes from the GIB and means the same segment on every node, such as a prefix segment bound to the End behavior. A local CSID comes from the LIB and means a different segment on each node, such as a non-routed adjacency segment bound to End.X. Two nodes may reuse the same local value for different SIDs.

For forwarding, a node instantiating a NEXT-CSID or REPLACE-CSID SID should install a FIB entry that matches only the Locator and Function parts, so that any Argument value is accepted. In the RFC's example, the NEXT-CSID End SID 2001:db8:b1:10:: gets the FIB entry 2001:db8:b1:10::/64.

The operational advice is to use the GIB mainly for global segments such as node SIDs, and the LIB for segments that identify services, cross-connects or adjacencies. Consistent LBL and CSID lengths within a routing domain keep compression efficient, and the two flavors can coexist in one SR domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Some short numbers mean the same place everywhere, like a famous landmark. Others only make sense on one street, like the third door on the left. The rules keep the two kinds apart.

sections.title: How the Source Node Compresses
sections.content:
The SR source node learns each SID's behavior and structure from the control plane or from configuration. Before compressing, it MUST validate each SID structure: LBL is not 0, LNFL is not 0, and AL equals 128-LBL-LNL-FL. An invalid structure is treated as unknown and is not compressible.

The source node MAY compress a SID list. The RFC gives one illustrative method that walks the list and packs consecutive NEXT-CSID SIDs, or consecutive REPLACE-CSID SIDs of the same CSID length, into containers. Any other method that is no longer is allowed, as long as the result expresses the same segments. Otherwise packets may be dropped or misrouted.

There are rules for each flavor. For REPLACE-CSID, all SIDs in a sequence MUST share the same Locator-Block and compression scheme, and all but the last MUST have the REPLACE-CSID flavor. For NEXT-CSID, an unused tail of an Argument MUST be zeros. Upper-layer checksums use the ultimate destination address in the pseudo-header.

On the control plane, the compressed behaviors are advertised like their base behaviors in IS-IS, OSPFv3, BGP, BGP-LS and PCEP. Signaling the SRv6 SID Structure is REQUIRED, and the advertised Argument bits MUST be 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Before shortening a list of directions, the sender checks that every address follows the rules. Then it packs the shareable parts together, and the result must still mean exactly the same trip.

sections.title: Compression Across Routing Domains
sections.content:
All CSIDs in one sequence share a Locator-Block. A path that crosses domains with different blocks would normally need a separate sequence for each. To avoid that, the RFC adds two behaviors that change the Locator-Block at the boundary: End.LBS (Locator-Block Swap) and End.XLBS (L3 cross-connect and Locator-Block Swap).

End.LBS is a variant of End, used when the domain boundary is on the endpoint node itself. End.XLBS is a variant of End.X, used when the boundary is on an adjacent link. Each is tied to a target Locator-Block B2/m, which is a local property of the SID. Both are defined with the NEXT-CSID and the REPLACE-CSID flavors, and the pseudocode builds the new Destination Address from B2 plus the remaining CSID data. How the source node learns B2 is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When the trip crosses into a new country, a border officer swaps the old city name for the new one. The short house numbers stay the same, so the sender does not need a second list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of Segment Routing (RFC 8402), the SRH (RFC 8754) and SRv6 network programming (RFC 8986), and says they apply here too.

Its argument is that nothing new is exposed. The paths a source node can enforce with a compressed list are the same, from a topology and service view, as those it could enforce with RFC 8986 SIDs. The new pseudocode changes how an endpoint finds the next SID, not the meaning of the active or next SID, and it does not change how the SID list itself is encoded in the packet. The document introduces no new SID semantic.
sections.plainLanguage: The new shorthand does not let anyone go anywhere they could not go before. It is the same trip written in fewer letters, so the old safety rules still work.
